newsitem.title: USA: US senators seek administrative remedy on CRP bill.
newsitem.headline: US senators seek administrative remedy on CRP bill.

text.p: Fourteen U.S. senators signed a letter that proposed an administrative remedy Wednesday for farmers who face planting deadlines but do not know if their land would be accepted for the Conservation Reserve Program.
An aide to Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar said the letter "outlines the agreement brokered by Senator Lugar to solve the CRP fall planting issue."
The Agriculture Department had no comment on the letter.
An administrative "fix" would end the chance of a legislative showdown. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman opposed a bill allowing unilateral extension of CRP contracts.

Reuters reported the three points of the letter on Tuesday: farmers should be allowed to begin field preparation without any loss of CRP rent, the senators would oppose any cap, like the one pending in the House, on new Conservation Reserve enrollments this year, and the senators opposed a White House proposal to defer some CRP enrollments to offset the cost of blocking a gold mine near Yellowstone National Park.
In the letter, senators stressed it was critical for USDA to notify farmers by late May if their land would be in CRP.
The House has passed a bill for unilateral extension of contracts for farmers with fall-planted crops.

"As you are well aware, growers whose offers are not accepted into the program will not have enough time nor the appropriate weather conditions to prepare their current CRP acreage for fall planting," they wrote. "We seek your prompt approval of ground preparation practices necessary for fall planting of winter crops on all expiring CRP acreas without loss of payments.
"Specifically, we request that producers be permitted to remove cover crops without penalty beginning immediately."

Signing the letter were Lugar and Iowan Tom Harkin, Democratic leader on the Agriculture Committee, along with Senators Slade Gorton, Washington state Republican; Larry Craig, Idaho Republican; Gordon Smith, Oregon Republican; Conrad Burns, Montana Republican; Dirk Kempthorne, Idaho Republican; Ron Wyden, Oregon Democrat; Patty Murray, Washington state Democrat; Pat Roberts, Kansas Republican; Sam Brownback, Kansas Republican; Max Baucus, Montana Democrat; Chuck Hegel, Nebraska Republican; and Michael Enzi, Wyoming Republican.
Contracts expire on 21 million acres this fall. Farmers have offered 25.6 million acres for enrollment. USDA has said it might accept up to 19 million acres this year.
